name: Community water systems serving the municipality
plain: How many community water systems serve each municipality: PRASA's systems and the community-run ones.
definition: Active community water systems that list the municipality among those they serve (EPA ECHO). A system serving several municipalities counts in each.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-11-11; EIA-860M of 2026-09). Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active community water systems of Puerto Rico and downloads seven columns. Each system counts in every municipality its FIPS codes name; 28 systems serve two to four municipalities and 5 small ones give no municipality (Puerto Rico's code only): they count in the island value only. Puerto Rico's value counts each system once, so the municipal values add up to more. The system's name is never kept.
source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_systems (p_st=PR, p_act=Y, p_systyp=CWS) and get_download, columns PWSId, PWSTypeCode, PopulationServedCount, OwnerTypeCode, SeriousViolator, HealthFlag, FIPSCodes
how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 404 active community water systems, which together serve about 3,295,853 people. The most are in Ponce 21, Caguas 20, Orocovis 18: municipalities with many small community-run systems.
caveats: The municipal values add up to more than Puerto Rico's, which counts each system once.
Population served is not given per municipality: a large system's people cannot be split honestly among the municipalities it serves.

name: Community water systems outside PRASA (non-PRASA)
plain: How many community water systems outside PRASA, most of them run by the community itself, serve each municipality.
definition: Active community water systems that the Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) records as privately owned, through EPA ECHO. EPA Region 2 defines the non-PRASA systems as the privately owned ones; most are run by community associations in the mountains, a few serve private developments or institutions. A system serving several municipalities counts in each.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-10-14). Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

method: infrastructure_series.py reads the owner type of each active community water system from the same ECHO download as water_systems and counts the privately owned ones (owner type P) in every municipality their FIPS codes name. Puerto Rico's value counts each system once. No name is kept.
source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_download, column OwnerTypeCode = P
how_to_read: 207 systems in Puerto Rico report serving 100,743 people. The most are in San Lorenzo 14, Orocovis 13, Caguas 13 and Utuado 12. 31 municipalities have none. 201 of the 207 carry ECHO's health-based violation flag (infrastructure_series.json notes).
caveats: SDWIS records some community-run systems as local government, the owner type of PRASA's systems, so this count can miss a few: EPA Region 2 counted 241 non-PRASA community systems serving about 93,500 people in 2025.

No federal source gives where these systems are below the municipality, and their names often carry a person's or a family's name, so the observatory publishes counts only (wanted.json: non-prasa-locations).
A violation flag is a compliance record, not proof that the water is unsafe today.

name: Residents served by community water systems outside PRASA
plain: How many people get their water from a community system outside PRASA, as the systems report it, in each municipality.
definition: The population that the non-PRASA systems (privately owned in SDWIS) report serving, added up for the systems that serve only this municipality. Shaded per 1,000 residents, it approximates the share of residents on a non-PRASA system.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-10-14). Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

method: infrastructure_series.py adds the PopulationServedCount of each non-PRASA system to its municipality when the system serves one municipality only. The 5 systems that serve two municipalities (1,087 people) and one that names no municipality (165 people) are left out of every municipality's value and counted in Puerto Rico's.
source_detail: ECHO sdw_rest_services get_download, columns PopulationServedCount, OwnerTypeCode = P, FIPSCodes
how_to_read: Puerto Rico: 100,743 people. Lares 17,278, Yabucoa 6,573, Naranjito 5,840, Caguas 4,958.
caveats: The population served is each system's own estimate to the regulator, not a census count.
The municipal values add up to less than Puerto Rico's: systems that serve two municipalities are left out of both, because their population cannot be split.
Systems recorded as local government are not included (see Community water systems outside PRASA).

name: Facilities with a permit to discharge wastewater
plain: How many facilities in each municipality hold their own federal permit to discharge wastewater into a river, a lake or the sea.
definition: Facilities with an active individual permit of the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), which EPA issues in Puerto Rico under the Clean Water Act: sewage treatment plants, water filtration plants, power plants, factories and others that discharge wastewater into surface waters, counted in the municipality that holds the facility's point.

coverage.frequency: One snapshot (ECHO of 2026-11-11; EIA-860M of 2026-09). Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

method: infrastructure_series.py searches ECHO for the active Clean Water Act facilities of Puerto Rico and downloads eight columns. It keeps the 177 facilities with an individual NPDES permit and leaves out the 1,097 facilities covered by a general permit (construction sites, industrial and municipal stormwater) and the records attached to another permit. Each facility counts once, in the municipality whose boundary holds its point; ECHO's own county code, taken from the mailing address, names another municipality for 6 of them. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the municipalities. The facility's name and point are never kept. Since 2026-11-12 the count is also given for the 901 barrios (infrastructure_barrio.json): a facility counts in the barrio whose outline holds its point, or the nearest outline within 2 km; 157 barrios hold one or more.
source_detail: ECHO cwa_rest_services get_facilities (p_st=PR, p_act=Y) and get_download, columns SourceID, FacFIPSCode, FacLat, FacLong, CWPFacilityTypeIndicator, CWPPermitTypeDesc, CWPMajorMinorStatusFlag, CWPStatus
how_to_read: Puerto Rico has 177 such facilities in 68 municipalities; the most in Peñuelas 9, Ponce 7, Utuado 7.
caveats: By barrio most counts are 0 or 1, so a barrio's figure often stands for a single facility. ECHO places a facility by the point on record, which can be a gate, an office or a mailing address rather than the works themselves, and at the scale of a barrio that can put it in the barrio next door.
A permit allows a discharge within limits; holding one is not a violation.
Construction sites and stormwater facilities covered by a general permit are not counted: they come and go with each project.
A facility counts where it stands. The water it discharges flows on to other municipalities downstream.
Septic tanks and discharges with no permit are not in ECHO.

name: Toxic chemicals released, pounds
plain: How many pounds of listed toxic chemicals the reporting facilities of each municipality released in a year.
definition: The pounds of listed toxic chemicals that the facilities reporting to EPA's Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) released in 2024: on site, to the air, to water and to land, and off site, sent elsewhere for disposal. Summed for the municipality that holds each facility's point.

coverage.frequency: One reporting year (2024), the newest EPA has published for Puerto Rico; EPA publishes a year in the autumn of the next. Rebuilt with each full build (python infrastructure_series.py).

method: infrastructure_series.py downloads EPA's TRI Basic Data File for Puerto Rico (reporting year 2024: 104 facilities), which has one row for each facility and chemical. It adds each facility's pounds (dioxins, reported in grams, are converted) and sums them for the municipality whose boundary holds the facility's point. Puerto Rico's value is the sum of the facilities. Values are whole pounds. The facility's name is never read, and its point is not published.

name: Highway bridges
plain: How many highway bridges are in each municipality, every year.
definition: Bridges of the public road network in the National Bridge Inventory (spans longer than 20 feet), in the municipality the inventory gives.

coverage.frequency: One inventory a year. FHWA publishes each year's file the following spring; the observatory adds it when FPR rebuilds the data.

method: infrastructure_series.py reads each year's Puerto Rico file and works out each bridge's condition by FHWA's rule (the lowest of the deck, superstructure, substructure and culvert ratings: 4 or below is poor, 7 or above good, the rest fair). In every year whose file gives FHWA's own condition column the two agree for every bridge; the build stops otherwise.
source_detail: FHWA National Bridge Inventory, delimited file PR{yy}.txt for 2016-2025: COUNTY_CODE_003, DECK_COND_058, SUPERSTRUCTURE_COND_059, SUBSTRUCTURE_COND_060, CULVERT_COND_062, BRIDGE_CONDITION
how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 2,308 bridges in 2016 and 2,434 in 2025.
caveats: New or newly inventoried bridges raise the count.

name: Air passengers boarding (commercial flights)
plain: How many passengers board a commercial flight at the airports of each municipality, every year.
definition: Passengers who boarded a commercial flight at an airport in the municipality during the year, to anywhere: the US mainland, another island or abroad. A passenger is counted each time they board.

coverage.frequency: Monthly at the source; the observatory publishes full years when FPR rebuilds the data (python gateway_series.py).

method: gateway_series.py sums BTS's monthly T-100 rows of the seven Puerto Rico airports in the file (SJU, BQN, PSE, VQS, CPX, SIG, MAZ) by year, and places each airport in the municipality that holds it (the FAA airports of transport.json): San Juan's Luis Muñoz Marín (SJU) is in Carolina and Isla Grande (SIG) in San Juan. A year is published once SJU has all twelve months.
source_detail: BTS T-100 Segment Summary by Origin Airport (data.bts.gov r495-tyji): total_passengers by origin_airport_code and month
how_to_read: 7.2 million passengers boarded at Puerto Rico's airports in 2025, 6.7 million of them at SJU (Carolina); in 2020 the figure fell to 2.5 million.
caveats: Counts boardings, not visitors: residents travelling and passengers changing planes are counted, and a passenger who arrives is not.
Ceiba's airport (RVR) is not in T-100; see the FAA count.
A smaller airport with fewer months in a year had no commercial flights in the others (Ponce reported 3 months in 2020 and 9 in 2021).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: air passengers boarding (commercial flights)

name: Commercial flights departing
plain: How many commercial flights leave the airports of each municipality, every year.
definition: Commercial flights, passenger and cargo, that departed from an airport in the municipality during the year.

coverage.frequency: Monthly at the source; the observatory publishes full years when FPR rebuilds the data (python gateway_series.py).

method: gateway_series.py sums BTS's monthly T-100 rows of the seven Puerto Rico airports in the file (SJU, BQN, PSE, VQS, CPX, SIG, MAZ) by year, and places each airport in the municipality that holds it (the FAA airports of transport.json): San Juan's Luis Muñoz Marín (SJU) is in Carolina and Isla Grande (SIG) in San Juan. A year is published once SJU has all twelve months.
source_detail: BTS T-100 Segment Summary by Origin Airport (data.bts.gov r495-tyji): total_departures by origin_airport_code and month
how_to_read: 94,613 commercial flights left Puerto Rico's airports in 2025, 68,110 of them from SJU.
caveats: Small island flights (Vieques, Culebra) carry few passengers each, so flights and passengers rank the airports differently.

name: Air passengers boarding (FAA enplanements)
plain: How many passengers board at the commercial airports of each municipality, as FAA counts them.
definition: Passengers who boarded at a commercial service airport in the municipality during the calendar year, as FAA counts them for airport funding. It includes Ceiba's airport (RVR) and on-demand air taxi flights.

coverage.frequency: One file a calendar year, published the following autumn; each file also holds the year before.

method: gateway_series.py reads every FAA file under its current name (CY2024 and CY2025, which give 2023 to 2025) and keeps Puerto Rico's rows; for a year two files share, the file of that year wins. Each airport is placed in its municipality as for T-100.
source_detail: FAA arp-cy{year}-commercial-service-enplanements.xlsx: Locid, ST, CY {yy} Enplanements
how_to_read: FAA counted 7.19 million boardings in 2025, within 0.1% of T-100's 7.20 million; Ceiba's 23,214 are only here.
caveats: Earlier years are in files under other names that no longer answer; the series starts in 2023.

name: Ferry passengers boarding
plain: How many passengers board a ferry at the terminals of each municipality, in the years of the ferry census.
definition: Passengers who boarded a ferry at a terminal in the municipality during the year the census covers, as the operator reported them: the Cataño crossing (Cataño and Old San Juan), Ceiba, Vieques and Culebra. Passengers going and coming back are each counted where they board.

coverage.frequency: Every two years (censuses of 2020, 2022 and 2024).

method: gateway_series.py reads each census's terminals in Puerto Rico, the one-way segments that start at them and the operator's passengers on each segment. A segment's passengers board at its first terminal, which is placed in the municipality that holds its point. The 2020 census gives data year 2019; since 2022 BTS names each census for the year of its data. The 2018 census is left out: it does not state its data year and its routes start at Fajardo, before the move to Ceiba.
source_detail: BTS NCFO operator segment, segment and terminal files of 2020, 2022 and 2024 (data.bts.gov): passengers, trips_per_year, seg_terminal1_id, terminal points
how_to_read: 1.62 million ferry boardings in 2024: 593,000 at Ceiba, 321,000 at Vieques, 273,000 at Culebra and 429,000 on the Cataño crossing.
caveats: Reported by the operator to the census, not counted by the observatory.
Only three years; the year control shows the latest census at or before the year chosen.
2022 was a year of reduced service on the Cataño crossing (84,145 and 86,441 boardings).
